competitive_landscape: Norway is the most marine-electrified nation on earth: battery-electric ferries are normal, charging norms exist, and public acceptance is high. Incumbents are converting displacement ferries to batteries — but those remain slow. Foiling's opening is to be both zero-emission AND markedly faster and smoother, turning a compliance upgrade into a service upgrade.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: Bergen's shorter fjord and commuter legs — Hardangerfjord (~35 nm), Osterfjord/Mostraumen (~22 nm), island commuter runs — sit inside the 70 nm all-electric envelope over flat, sheltered fjord water, exactly the conditions foiling loves, and directly satisfy the 2026 zero-emission mandate.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Carries the long scenic line-haul — Bergen↔Flåm/inner Sognefjord (~90 nm) and coastal express corridors — beyond the all-electric range with no dependence on charging infrastructure at small fjord-head villages.

regulatory_note: The Norwegian Maritime Authority and the Storting have set a zero-emission requirement in the UNESCO World Heritage fjords from 2026, with broader fjord coverage progressing. This is the strongest pro-electric regulatory tailwind of any market in the atlas — clean propulsion is becoming the license to operate, not merely a differentiator.
seasonality: Fjord tourism peaks May-September (midnight-sun months and cruise season); commuter demand is year-round. Winter brings short days and cold but the fjords are sheltered; the zero-emission mandate applies regardless of season, sustaining a year-round compliance-driven market.

summary: Bergen is the capital of the Norwegian fjords and the gateway to Sognefjord, Hardangerfjord and the wider UNESCO World Heritage fjord landscape that draws roughly 6 million Fjord Norway visitors a year. Norway has already electrified much of its public ferry network — over NOK 3.8 billion invested, dozens of battery-electric ferries in service — and from 1 January 2026 a zero-emission requirement takes effect in the UNESCO World Heritage fjords (Geirangerfjord and Nærøyfjord), with the broader fjord network following. That mandate turns clean propulsion from a nice-to-have into a license-to-operate. Bergen's protected, deep, sheltered fjord waters and dense tourist-plus-commuter demand make it an ideal launch theatre for foiling vessels that are not just zero-emission but faster and smoother than the displacement ferries they'd replace.
tagline: Norway has made zero-emission the law in its World Heritage fjords from 2026 — and Bergen is the gateway to all of them. The regulatory tailwind here is the strongest on earth.
